strengths: Well-motivated problem: identifies genuine gap between separate treatment of continuous trajectories and discrete events in existing methods
Technically sound approach: factorized diffusion formulation with proper mathematical framework and reasonable independence assumptions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple datasets, tasks, human evaluation, detailed ablations (discrete steps, λ weighting, attention entropy)
Strong execution quality: well-organized presentation, extensive appendices, clear implementation details, architectural diagrams
Novel controllability interface: weak-possessor-guidance elegantly enables flexible high-level control without rigid timing constraints
Consistent empirical results: achieves SOTA across multiple metrics and datasets (SADE improvements in imputation: 13-19%)
Good reproducibility: detailed architecture, hyperparameters, baseline implementations documented
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: joint continuous-discrete diffusion is not new (Levi et al. 2023, Chereddy & Femiani 2025); primarily applies existing techniques to sports domain with simplistic possession events
Unclear joint modeling benefit: ablation shows only 3-5% improvements; Table 6 shows λ=0.1 optimal with low discrete loss weight—questions whether joint training is necessary vs. helpful

Domain-specific scope with no generalization evidence: all experiments on sports (NBA, NFL, BundesLiga); no demonstration of transfer to autonomous driving, pedestrian forecasting, or robotics; possession event structure is sport-specific
Small datasets limiting confidence: BundesLiga only 2,093 scenes (~4k augmented); authors acknowledge small data hurts text-guidance quality; insufficient for robust deep generative model training
Weak controllability validation: WPG accuracy modest (NBA 0.87/0.67 max/avg); text-guidance only on 2/3 datasets with visible failures; no user studies on controllability satisfaction
Human evaluation limitations: only 15 participants with ~130-150 comparisons per pair; 53% win vs w/o joint not overwhelming; 44% loss vs ground truth and 24% ties suggest evaluator uncertainty

Design choices lack justification: different samplers for continuous (DDIM) vs discrete (stochastic) unexplained; hybrid Sd schedule presented as empirical without theoretical grounding; CrossGuid modality-specific variants not ablated

Strong forward process independence assumption (Eq. 2): discrete events directly influence continuous motion (e.g., passes), but method assumes independent noising—potentially limiting despite reverse network learning dependencies
Missing critical baselines: no comparison to separately trained models with post-hoc synchronization; no comparison to trajectory-correction methods; incomplete recent method comparisons
Text annotation quality concerns: semi-automatic generation via rule-based rules + LLM post-processing; no human evaluation of description quality; potential systematic biases in generated captions

Incomplete evaluation: no error bars/confidence intervals; no statistical significance testing; no sensitivity analysis for design choices (e.g., 1.5m possession threshold); no scalability analysis with agent count/sequence length

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap in trajectory generation where continuous motion and discrete events must be modeled jointly
Technically sound joint continuous-discrete diffusion framework with rigorous mathematical formulation and proper loss decomposition

Comprehensive experimental validation across three sports datasets with multiple evaluation metrics (scene-level SADE/SFDE, individual-level ADE/FDE, event accuracy), human evaluation, and extensive ablations
Novel controllable guidance mechanisms (weak-possessor-guidance and text-guidance) with CrossGuid as a clean architectural contribution for multi-modal conditioning
Strong empirical results achieving SOTA on average metrics (e.g., 2.36/3.40 SADE/SFDE on NFL) with human preference studies showing 65-80% win rates against baselines
Practical contribution of annotated sports benchmarks with text descriptions and commitment to release code, aiding reproducibility and community benefit
Interpretability analysis showing joint modeling maintains more focused attention patterns (Fig. 8) and improves scene coherence beyond trajectory accuracy

Restrictive problem scope limited to dense, structured events; cannot handle sparse events or point processes; only possession events modeled; unclear generalization to other domains (autonomous driving, robotics)

Dataset quality concerns including small sizes (~10k NFL, ~2k BundesLiga), heuristic-based event extraction (1.5m threshold, not ground truth), missing player identification in NFL, and LLM-generated synthetic text captions rather than human annotations
Incomplete text-guidance evaluation with only qualitative examples, no quantitative faithfulness metrics, missing NBA results in Table 2, and acknowledged robustness issues due to limited data

Technical justification gaps including: untested independence assumption (Eq. 2) potentially too restrictive, hybrid sampling strategy lacks theoretical grounding, discrete step reduction S_d=10 'empirically found' without sensitivity analysis

Limited baseline comparisons with no direct evaluation against other joint continuous-discrete methods, single ablation variant (Ours w/o joint), and missing quantitative metrics for generated event realism beyond guidance accuracy

strengths: Well-motivated problem: addresses a genuine gap in jointly modeling continuous trajectories and discrete events in multi-agent systems
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple datasets, tasks, baselines, ablations, and human studies demonstrating consistent improvements
Technically sound approach: principled joint continuous-discrete diffusion framework with multinomial diffusion empirically shown superior to absorbing state for dynamic domains
Practical contributions: two novel controllable generation modes (weak-possessor-guidance and text-guidance) with intuitive user interfaces
Appropriate evaluation metrics: uses scene-level SADE/SFDE metrics and validates against individual-level metrics through human evaluation
Strong empirical results: achieves state-of-the-art on most benchmarks with human preference studies showing clear wins (80% vs MoFlow, 65% vs U2Diff)
Thorough documentation: extensive appendices with architecture details, ablations, qualitative results, and commitment to release code/data
Interpretability: attention entropy analysis demonstrates joint modeling enables more focused agent interactions
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: architecture reuses U2Diff, CrossGuid module is straightforward attention-based conditioning, multinomial diffusion is an application of existing techniques rather than a new method

Severely limited event modeling scope: restricted to dense, structured categorical events aligned with spatio-temporal trajectories; cannot handle sparse/asynchronous events or point processes, limiting applicability beyond sports

Narrow domain focus: only evaluated on sports with unclear generalization to other multi-agent systems (autonomous driving, robotics, pedestrian forecasting); scope appears domain-specific rather than broadly applicable
Small training datasets: ~10k NFL pairs, ~2k Bundesliga (4k augmented) limit model robustness; acknowledged text-guidance inconsistencies stem from insufficient data variety
Modest empirical improvements in some cases: NFL SADE improvement over U2Diff (3.74→3.40) is marginal; min metrics sometimes lag behind non-IID baselines; gains become smaller on imputation tasks

Incomplete text-guidance evaluation: no baselines for text conditioning beyond w/o joint variant; no explicit alignment metrics; failure cases shown but not systematically analyzed; NBA dataset has no text annotations
Insufficient human evaluation scale: only 15 participants, 128 samples, no inter-rater agreement or statistical significance tests reported

Underdeveloped technical justification: conditional independence assumption (Eq. 5) stated without discussing approximation quality; hybrid schedule choice (Sd, ζ ratio) empirically driven without theoretical grounding; λ=0.1 optimality not well explained
Generated text descriptions: automated pipeline + LLM post-processing, not human-curated; limits reliability for text-guidance evaluation

Limited failure analysis: only two failure examples shown; unclear when/why method fails beyond 'limited data variety'; no systematic analysis of event types or trajectory characteristics causing failures

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three datasets with human studies and extensive ablations
Technically sound mathematical framework for joint continuous-discrete diffusion
Well-documented implementation with thorough appendix including qualitative results and failure cases
Useful practical contributions: benchmark with text annotations and two novel controllable generation tasks (WPG and text-guidance)
Addresses a genuine gap in modeling continuous trajectories and discrete events jointly
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Joint continuous-discrete diffusion via factorization and conditional independence is a straightforward extension of prior work (Levi et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025)

Unconvincing benefits of joint modeling: Table 2 shows negligible improvements (e.g., NBA text-guidance 2.19→2.08 SADE); human evaluation shows only 53% preference over non-joint variant without ties, contradicting claims that joint modeling is 'crucial'

Narrow applicability: Possession events extracted via simple 1.5m heuristic; strong assumptions require events as categorical variables aligned with trajectories; cannot handle sparse or asynchronous events
Modest empirical gains: Marginal improvements across datasets (NFL 2.36→2.59 SADE, Bundesliga 2.47→2.69, NBA 1.39→1.48) that don't justify added architectural complexity

Weak controllability: WPG is trivial (just player ID sequences); text-guidance unreliable with acknowledged failure cases (Fig. 14), limited to 2/3 datasets, and hindered by small dataset sizes (~2k Bundesliga, ~10k NFL)
Questionable metric arguments: SADE/SFDE inherently favor IID strategies and are not neutral metrics; claim of superiority over ADE/FDE lacks rigorous justification

Dataset and evaluation concerns: Small training sets (≈2k Bundesliga), heuristic-based event labels (NFL), limited human evaluation (15 participants, 15 pairs), no statistical significance testing, cherry-picked modes for evaluation

Unjustified architectural choices: CrossGuid applies updates asymmetrically for WPG vs. text without justification; DDIM for continuous but stochastic sampling for discrete lacks rationale; hybrid schedule (Sd<S) appears ad-hoc
Incomplete ablations: No exploration of conditional independence assumptions, different conditioning strategies, or why multinomial enables 'continuous refinement' versus absorbing state

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First to unify continuous trajectory and discrete event generation in temporally-evolving multi-agent systems; addresses genuine gap in existing literature

Technically sound joint diffusion framework: Mathematically well-derived with proper factorization and posterior analysis; choice of multinomial over absorbing state diffusion well-justified and empirically validated (Table 3)
Comprehensive experimental validation: Multi-dataset evaluation (NBA, NFL, Bundesliga), multiple metrics (SADE/SFDE, accuracy, human evaluation), and extensive ablations across key hyperparameters
Strong and consistent empirical results: State-of-the-art on completion generation (13-19% improvement), human preference (80% vs MoFlow, 65% vs U2Diff), improvements across all datasets

Novel controllability methods: Weak-possessor-guidance enables intuitive semantic control without rigid timing; text-guidance introduces new capability for multi-agent systems with modality-specific CrossGuid implementations
Thorough consistency analysis: Table 3 rigorously validates trajectory-event coherence, demonstrating joint modeling ensures coherent outputs beyond individual metrics
High reproducibility: Detailed architecture specs, dataset generation procedures, hyperparameter specifications, and commitment to release code/data
weaknesses: Limited event scope: Framework models only possession events (single categorical per timestep); cannot handle diverse event types (passes, tackles, shots) or sparse temporal point processes; generalization to other domains unclear

Unvalidated independence assumptions: Eq. 2 assumes independent Y and E noise processes without empirical validation; conditional independence (Eq. 5) made for tractability but not ablated; coupled vs. factorized processes not compared

Dataset limitations for text-guidance: Text descriptions are auto-generated via rule-based templates + LLM post-processing, not human-annotated; only ~2-10k pairs; acknowledged failure cases (Fig. 14) due to limited data variety reduce confidence in text-guidance component

Modest architectural novelty: Base architecture largely from U2Diff; CrossGuid is standard multi-head attention with agent embeddings; main contribution is problem formulation rather than methodological innovation
Small-scale human evaluation: Only 15 participants on 128 past observations; no confidence intervals; single-domain (sports) validation limits generalization claims

Hyperparameter choices lack justification: Shared variance schedule for continuous/discrete processes is arbitrary; hybrid schedule introduces tuning (S_d=10 for S=50); λ=0.1 ablated but theoretical motivation absent

Evaluation gaps: No comparison with other joint continuous-discrete approaches; no computational cost analysis; SADE/SFDE improvements clear but still limitations as comprehensive scene quality metrics

Text-guidance limited to templated descriptions: Restricted to event-centric language (player X passes to Y), not free-form natural language; unclear if approach scales to richer, longer descriptions or out-of-distribution text
